course.title: Mathematical Foundations for Data Science
course.description:
The mathematics you need before machine learning, in three connected parts: **Linear Algebra** (linear systems, matrices, determinants, eigenvalues, vector spaces, linear mappings), **Calculus and Optimization** (functions, derivatives, the chain rule, partial derivatives, gradients, gradient descent) and **Probability and Statistics** (conditional probability, Bayes' rule, random variables, distributions, expectation, variance, joint distributions, sampling, estimation and confidence intervals).

15 topics · about 45 hours (15 class hours + 30 hours of independent study). Each topic has worked examples, practice questions with feedback on the exact misconception behind a wrong answer, and flashcards for spaced review. Lecture notes and slides for every part are attached as PDFs.

lessons.body:
Machine learning is applied mathematics. A model is a function with parameters, training is optimisation of those parameters, and the data it learns from is uncertain. This course gives you exactly the three mathematical languages behind that sentence — **linear algebra** for representing data and transformations, **calculus** for measuring change and optimising, and **probability and statistics** for reasoning under uncertainty.

> [!ghi-nho] The emphasis is on **mathematical reasoning and interpretation in data science and machine learning contexts**, not on memorising formulas. When you finish a topic you should be able to say what an object *means* (a matrix as a transformation, a gradient as the direction of steepest increase, a confidence interval as a statement about a procedure) and when to use it.

## Course facts

| | |
|---|---|
| Class contact | 15 hours |
| Independent study | 30 hours |
| Total workload | 45 hours |
| Structure | 3 parts · 15 topics |

## The three parts

| Part | Module | Class hours | Topics |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | Linear Algebra | 5 | 1 Linear systems · 2 Matrix operations and inverses · 3 Determinants · 4 Eigenvalues and eigenvectors · 5 Vector spaces and linear mappings |
| II | Calculus and Optimization for Machine Learning | 5 | 6 Functions, exponentials and logarithms · 7 Derivatives, chain rule and marginal effects · 8 Partial derivatives and the gradient · 9 Optimization and gradient descent |
| III | Introduction to Probability and Statistics | 5 | 10 Probability foundations · 11 Random variables and distributions · 12 Expectation, variance and moments · 13 Joint distributions and dependence · 14 Sampling distributions and the CLT · 15 Estimation and confidence intervals |

## Learning outcomes

By the end of the course you can:

- **LO.1 (Understand)** Explain the concepts and terminology of linear algebra, calculus and optimization, and probability and statistics.
- **LO.2 (Understand)** Explain the structure and solution of linear systems and the main properties and operations of matrices.
- **LO.3 (Understand)** Explain determinants, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, vector spaces and linear mappings.
- **LO.4 (Understand)** Explain functions, limits, derivatives, the chain rule, marginal effects, partial derivatives and gradients.
- **LO.5 (Apply)** Apply derivatives and gradients to analyse functions and basic optimization problems, including gradient descent.
- **LO.6 (Apply)** Apply probability rules, conditional probability, independence, the law of total probability and Bayes' rule.
- **LO.7 (Apply)** Work with random variables, mass and density functions, cumulative distributions, common distributions, expectation and variance.
- **LO.8 (Analyze)** Analyse joint, marginal and conditional distributions, dependence, covariance, correlation and conditional expectation.
- **LO.9 (Analyze)** Analyse sampling distributions and estimators using bias, variance, mean square error, confidence intervals, efficiency and consistency.
- **LO.10 (Evaluate)** Select and justify the mathematical concepts and procedures that suit a structured data science or machine learning problem.

## How you are assessed

| Component | Weight | What it looks like | LOs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quiz / short analytical test | 20% | Short-answer and problem-based questions on definitions, calculations and interpretation | LO.1–LO.7 |
| Problem-solving assignment | 30% | Structured problems from all three parts, with your reasoning explained | LO.2–LO.9 |
| Integrated final assessment | 50% | Scenarios where you choose and apply methods from the whole course | LO.2–LO.10 |

The quizzes in this course follow the first component: every wrong answer is linked to a specific misconception, and the feedback tells you *where the reasoning went wrong*, not just that it did.

## How to study each topic

1. Read the lesson and **try each worked example yourself before opening the next step**.
2. Do the topic quiz. Rate your confidence before you see the answer — knowing that you are unsure is information.
3. Review the flashcards the next day, then a week later.
4. Read the lecture notes PDF for the full derivations and look at the slides before class.

## Recommended resources

The lecture notes and slides attached to each part are the primary text. For further reading, see the textbooks listed in the syllabus (Strang, *Introduction to Linear Algebra*; Boyd & Vandenberghe, *Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra*; Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, *Mathematics for Machine Learning*; Wasserman, *All of Statistics*).
summary: The course has three parts and fifteen topics; each part is five class hours.
Quizzes (20%), the problem-solving assignment (30%) and the integrated final assessment (50%) together test LO.1–LO.10.
Study by attempting every step yourself first, using the quiz confidence rating, and reviewing flashcards on a spaced schedule.
